extracted.intended_audience: college and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, higher-education legal counsel, compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for postsecondary institutions on selecting and applying standards of evidence and related procedural requirements in Title IX grievance processes (e.g., burden of proof, applicability across students/employees, prompt/equitable resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible standards of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final regulations recipients may select either the preponderance of the evidence standard or the clear and convincing evidence standard for resolving Title IX formal complaints (§106.45(b)(7)(i) and related discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes either standard may be applied because both are consistent with Title IX's non-discrimination and due process protections. The selection should reflect the degree of confidence the recipient expects decision-makers to have when reaching determinations regarding responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on standards higher than clear and convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not permitted to select a standard of evidence higher than clear and convincing (for example, the criminal 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard is not allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reasons explained in the rulemaking, the Department limits permissible standards to the two listed (preponderance and clear and convincing) and disallows higher criminal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof rests on the recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final regulations, §106.45(b)(5)(i), the burden of proof rests on the recipient, not on the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must ensure their procedures and decision-makers reflect that the institution carries the burden to reach determinations, rather than requiring parties (complainant or respondent) to carry that burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must disclose the selected standard of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department believes that all complainants who file formal complaints should have the benefit of understanding the recipient's decision on the issue of standard of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should publish and otherwise communicate which standard they use so complainants and respondents know the degree of confidence decision-makers must have. This disclosure supports transparency and predictability in grievance processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of standard regardless of respondent status
rubrics_metrics.description: Different 'degrees of confidence' should not be applied based on a respondent's status as a student or employee because whether the respondent is a student or employee does not necessarily alter the nature of the harm or lessen seriousness of potential consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should not automatically adopt different evidentiary thresholds solely because the respondent is faculty/staff versus a student; the regulations allow selection of one of the two standards, but application should be justified and not based merely on status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must respond promptly and without deliberate indifference upon actual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(a) requires a recipient with actual knowledge of sexual harassment in the recipient's education program or activity against a person in the United States to respond promptly in a manner that is not deliberately indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grievance processes and institutional actions should be timely and substantive; failure to act promptly or acting with deliberate indifference can violate Title IX obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance procedures must provide for prompt and equitable resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final regulations (revising 34 CFR 106.8(b)), recipients must have grievance procedures that provide for the prompt and equitable resolution of complaints from students and employees alleging sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should be written and implemented to ensure fairness and timeliness; dissemination of policy and procedural revisions is addressed elsewhere in the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of supportive measures after non-responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prevents a recipient from providing supportive measures to a complainant even after a determination of non-responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions retain discretion to offer services (e.g., counseling, academic adjustments) regardless of the outcome, to address needs of complainants and the campus community.

rubrics_metrics.name: No corroboration requirement for meeting evidentiary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts do not impose a requirement of corroborating evidence with respect to meeting either the preponderance of the evidence or clear and convincing evidence standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and decision-makers need not require independent corroboration as a gatekeeping rule; the chosen standard is applied to the totality of admissible and relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of selecting a standard: degree of confidence instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard of proof instructs the factfinder concerning the degree of confidence our society thinks he should have in the correctness of factual conclusions for a particular type of adjudication (In re Winship and related citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing between standards, institutions should consider what degree of confidence they expect decision-makers to have given the seriousness of the allegations and potential consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection should reflect recipient's legal, cultural, and pedagogical needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations permit recipients to select between these standards to best meet the legal, cultural, and pedagogical needs of the recipient's community with respect to the degree of certainty expected of decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may weigh community values, legal context (including applicable state law or CBAs), and educational mission when choosing which standard to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to reconcile evidentiary standard with collective bargaining agreements (CBAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach in these final regulations may help recipients address challenges reconciling CBAs that require a different (usually higher) standard of evidence by allowing recipients to select one of two reasonable options regarding a standard of evidence for Title IX purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should review CBAs and may use the permitted options to align Title IX processes with bargaining obligations where possible; some CBAs include clauses subordinating agreement provisions to federal law, which may affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different types of misconduct may justify different evidentiary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements of different claim types (for example, research misconduct requires intentionality while the §106.30 definition of sexual harassment does not) may justify using different standards of evidence for different types of allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may reasonably apply different standards across distinct institutional processes where the nature and elements of misconduct differ, but should document and justify such distinctions consistent with Title IX and other applicable laws.
